---
title: "R interop"
guide-section: "Guide"
---

The process at the other end of a channel does not have to be Python.
[mizu](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mizu) is the R binding of the same
shared-memory core, and a channel or pool connects the two languages
directly.

## R channel peers

A channel peer can be an R process with the `mizu` package installed.
Pass the peer program as R source, and set the launcher to
`pymizu.r_launcher()`:

```python
import pymizu

ch = pymizu.Channel.create(
    """
library(mizu)
repeat {
  x <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
  if (inherits(x, "mizu_sentinel")) break
  mizu_send(ch, x)
}
""",
    launcher=pymizu.r_launcher(),
)

import numpy as np
ch.send(np.array([1.5, 2.5, 3.5]))   # arrives in R as a numeric vector
print(ch.recv(timeout=5))            # echoes back as a float64 array
ch.close()
```

`r_launcher()` needs R and the `mizu` R package installed.
If either is missing, it raises `MizuError` before the channel is created.
Pass `rscript=` to use a specific R installation.

To spawn the peer differently, write your own launcher: one callable that
takes the channel's token and starts the peer process.
The reverse direction works too — an R session spawns a Python peer with
`mizu::mizu_py_launcher()`.

## Mixed-language pools

A pool's workers can be R processes.
`pymizu.r_pool_launcher()` spawns them, and `pymizu.call()` describes the
task: a qualified function name (`"pkg::fn"` for R, `"mod.fn"` for Python) or
a `source=` string, plus constant arguments:

```python
import numpy as np
import pymizu

pool = pymizu.Pool.create(4, launcher=pymizu.r_pool_launcher())
t = pool.submit(pymizu.call("stats::quantile", np.arange(101.0),
                            probs=np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]), names=False))
print(t.collect())                  # [ 25.  50.  75.]
t2 = pool.submit(pymizu.call(source="y <- x * 2\ny + 1", x=20))
print(t2.collect())                 # 41
pool.stop()
```

Unnamed arguments become positional arguments, and keyword arguments become
named ones, matching R's calling convention.
A `source=` task evaluates in a fresh environment with the keyword arguments
bound as names and the positional arguments bound as `_1`, `_2`, ...
The result is the value of the last expression.

The workers' language comes from the pool itself — there is no language
argument and no override.
On an R-worker pool, submitting a plain Python callable raises an error
naming `pymizu.call()`.
An unqualified name errors at submit.
An argument that cannot cross the boundary raises `DeclinedError` at submit.
An error in the R code crosses as `TaskError` with the R error type preserved
in `remote_type`.
A result with no Python equivalent fails the task with an error naming the
type.
The reverse direction mirrors: `mizu::mizu_pool()` with
`mizu::mizu_py_pool_launcher()`, and `mizu::mizu_submit_call()` with
`mizu::mizu_call()` specs.

Large arguments cross without copying.
A fresh array argument past the zero-copy floor (a fixed size threshold) is
written to shared memory once — one layout write — and the worker reads a
view over it.
An argument that is already a shared view (a `_ShmView`, or a numpy array
whose `.base` chain ends in one) crosses as its identifier alone — zero
payload bytes.
If the pool runs workers too old to read such references, the submit fails
with an error naming the remedy.
A pool's workers all run one language: mixing R and Python workers in one
pool is not supported.

## Mapping over a foreign pool

A `pymizu.call()` spec is also a map's `fn` — `Pool.map()` and
`Pool.map_prepare()` on an R-worker pool (and `mizu::mizu_map()` mirrors this
in R):

```python
pool = pymizu.Pool.create(4, launcher=pymizu.r_pool_launcher())
pool.map(pymizu.call("stats::median"), x)
pool.map(pymizu.call(source="summary(mgcv::gam(x$y ~ s(x$x)))$r.sq"),
         folds, template=0.0)   # each fold a dict; the element binds as x
pool.stop()
```

Each element fills the spec's first positional argument (a named spec) or
binds as `x` (a `source=` spec).
Put constant arguments in the spec itself: the map's own `args=`/`kwargs=`
must stay empty.
`template=` and `collect=` work unchanged, and a per-element error crosses
with its `index`.
Spec maps take integer seeds only (within R's 32-bit range when the workers
are R).
Each language derives its own random streams from the seed, so results are
reproducible for a given worker language but not identical across languages.

## What crosses the language boundary

A portable subset of values crosses in both directions:

- Python scalars (`bool`, `int`, `float`, `complex`, `str`, `None`), lists,
  and dicts with `str` keys cross both ways.
  R sees its own logical, integer, double, complex, character, and list
  values.
  A `tuple` arrives as a `list`.
- A 1-D contiguous numpy array of any fixed-width numeric dtype arrives as an
  R vector, and an R vector arrives as a numpy array.
  See the [dtype matrix](#the-dtype-matrix) below for the exact
  correspondence.
- A large array crosses without copying: each side reads the other's vector
  as a view over the shared pages.
  Without numpy, a received view is a buffer exporter, and any Arrow
  consumer wraps the shared pages zero-copy through the Arrow PyCapsule
  protocol: `pa.array(view)`, `pl.from_arrow(view)`.
- A multi-dimensional numpy array arrives as an R array with `dim` set (a
  matrix is the 2-D case) — C order, F order, strided, it crosses
  value-exact.
  A large Fortran-order array also crosses without copying — R reads a matrix
  view over the shared pages; C-order and strided arrays cross by copy.
  `datetime64` arrays with day or week units arrive as `Date`, and finer
  units arrive as `POSIXct`.
  `datetime.date` and `datetime.datetime` scalars arrive as the length-1
  forms.
- An Arrow array arrives as an R vector, with Arrow nulls as R missing
  values: `ch.send(pa.array([1, None, 3]))`.
  Anything with `__arrow_c_array__` works (pyarrow, polars, a duckdb result
  column).
- An Arrow stream — a polars or pandas DataFrame, a pyarrow Table or
  ChunkedArray, a polars Series, a duckdb relation, anything with
  `__arrow_c_stream__` — arrives as an R `data.frame`.
  Dictionary-encoded columns become factors, and `date32`/`timestamp` columns
  become `Date`/`POSIXct`.
  A Series arrives as a plain vector.
  An R `data.frame` arrives as a `pymizu.Frame` (below), and a factor as
  `list[str | None]`.
- `bytes` arrives as an R raw vector.
- Strings cross both ways.
  R's `NA_character_` arrives as `None`, and a string vector arrives as
  `list[str | None]`.
  A large `list[str | None]` sent to R also crosses without copying — R reads
  a character vector over the shared pages, with `None` as `NA_character_`.
- A value outside the portable subset raises `pymizu.DeclinedError` (a
  subclass of `TypeError`) at send time, with `path` and `reason` attributes
  naming what was rejected and why.

## pymizu.Frame

A `pymizu.Frame` is Python's home for an R `data.frame`: named columns with a
row count.
`frame.to_dict()` returns the columns as a dict — numpy arrays when numpy is
installed, memoryviews otherwise, strings and factors as `list[str | None]`.
`frame.names` and `frame.row_names` carry the metadata.
Any Arrow consumer takes a frame in one line — `pl.from_arrow(f)`,
`pa.table(f)`, `pd.DataFrame.from_arrow(f)`.
Factors become dictionary columns, logicals Arrow `bool`, `Date` `date32`,
and `POSIXct` `timestamp[us]`.
A `Frame` pickles, so it crosses Python-to-Python channels.
Sent to R, it becomes a `data.frame` again.

## Data frames without copying

- A large `data.frame` (past 32 KB) crosses as one shared-memory region in
  either direction.
  Python receives a region-backed `Frame`: its columns read directly from the
  shared pages, numeric columns as read-only numpy views.
  R receives an ordinary `data.frame`, read in place.
- If the other side is too old to read these regions, the frame crosses as a
  copy instead — the value always arrives.
- Sending a received frame back unmodified moves no data at all: it crosses
  as a reference to the region it arrived from.
  This holds through polars or pyarrow (`pl.from_arrow(f)`, `pa.table(f)`)
  as long as no column was modified.
- Modifying some columns moves only those columns.
  Each unmodified column still crosses as a reference, so a relay that adds
  one computed column pays for one column.
  R reads the unmodified columns as views of the original region.
- A polars or pyarrow object that wraps a received frame keeps the frame's
  shared-memory region alive until it is deleted and garbage-collected.
  Holding many of them at once can force later sends back to copying, so
  delete them when they are no longer needed.

## Dates, times, and other types

- A factor crosses as `list[str | None]` on its own, or as a
  dictionary-encoded column inside a frame.
- A `Date` crosses as `datetime64[D]` or Arrow `date32`.
  A `POSIXct` crosses as a naive `datetime64[us]` or `timestamp[us, tz]`:
  microsecond precision, `NaT` read as `NA`.
  A named timezone is kept as frame column metadata but dropped from a
  standalone vector.
  Naive Python datetimes arrive in R with `tzone = "UTC"`.
- A `difftime` crosses as `timedelta64[us]`: microsecond precision, `NA`
  read as `NaT`.
  R's five units cross by value; a round trip normalizes them to seconds.
  `timedelta64` arrays of any non-calendar unit cross likewise (numpy
  scalars and `datetime.timedelta` included).
  Inside a frame, a difftime column exports to Arrow as `duration[us]`,
  and an Arrow `duration` column arrives as a difftime.
- A `POSIXlt`, Arrow
  `date64`/`time`/`interval`, and ordered dictionaries (polars
  Enums) are declined at send time.
- An R vector with `names` is declined (numpy has no per-element names).
  A matrix crosses with values exact — the data is never transposed.
  `dimnames` and character matrices are declined.
- Cross-language sends copy R's ALTREP vectors by value: exact values, the
  compact representation is not preserved.

## The dtype matrix

The exact correspondence between Python and R dtypes.
Conversion happens once, at send time.
The identity rows (float64, int32, int64, complex128, uint8) are a plain
memcpy.

| Python sends | R receives | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| `bytes` / uint8 | raw | Arrow uint8 with nulls: `TypeError` (R raw has no NA) |
| int8 / int16 / uint16 | integer | widened, exact |
| int32 | integer | |
| uint32 | double | widened, exact |
| int64 | integer64 (bit64's layout) | bit-exact; `INT64_MIN` reads as `NA` |
| uint64 | double | exact to ±2^53; past it, `NA` plus one warning |
| float32 / float64 | double | |
| bool | logical | |
| complex64 / complex128 | complex | (buffer protocol only; Arrow has no standard complex) |
| Arrow bool / numeric with nulls | logical / numeric with `NA` | the validity bitmap is honored, slices included |
| Arrow strings (utf8 / large_utf8 / string_view) | character | a Series arrives as `list[str \| None]`; a column as a frame column |
| Arrow `date32` / `timestamp[u]` | `Date` / `POSIXct` | the zone name rides a frame column's metadata |
| Arrow `duration[u]` | `difftime` (secs) | the unit converts to seconds; the frame column exports back as `duration[us]` |
| timedelta64 (any non-calendar unit) | `difftime` (secs) | `NaT` reads as `NA`; the unit converts to seconds |
| Arrow dictionary-encoded | factor | an ordered dictionary declines (`polars Enum`: cast to `pl.Categorical`) |
| Arrow ChunkedArray / Table / Series | vector / `data.frame` | chunks are concatenated |
| Arrow nested, decimal, time32/64, interval | — | `DeclinedError` at send time |

Missing values:

- R marks missing values with sentinels inside the data: `INT_MIN` for
  integer and logical, `INT64_MIN` for integer64, and a special NaN value
  (`NA_real_`) for double.
  Arrow nulls convert to these sentinels, so R sees correct `NA`s.
- Read from Python, the result depends on the accessor:
  - Copied reads (`list(...)`, `Frame.to_dict()`) give honest dtypes: a
    logical arrives as `bool_` when it has no `NA`, else int32; an integer
    arrives as int32 when `NA`-free, else float64 with NaN (every int32 value
    is exact in float64).
  - Zero-copy views keep the sentinel values in the buffer.
    `.to_numpy()` applies the same rule, reading NA-freeness off the
    region's validity section before any data scan.
  - int64 keeps its dtype in every numpy form and warns when an `NA` is
    detected on a copied read or `.to_numpy()`.
    Use `.to_arrow()` for an NA-honest read.
    A genuine Python `-2^63` value round-trips without a warning.
  - Every Arrow export of a logical is Arrow `bool` with a validity bitmap,
    whatever the path.
    Integer exports are int32 or int64 with a validity bitmap.
- A genuine int32 value of `-2147483648` collides with the `NA` sentinel and
  reads as `NA` in R.
  Likewise an int64 value of `-9223372036854775808` reads as `NA_integer64_`.
  numpy sends stay silent.
  An Arrow int32 send with a validity bitmap warns once.
- Python compute treats `NA_real_` as an ordinary NaN.
  Whether the exact NaN value survives arithmetic is platform-dependent — do
  not rely on it.

Round trips are stable after the first hop, and a pass-through echo is
bit-exact: an untouched received view sent back crosses as a reference to its
region — no data moves — so even the `NA_real_` value survives a relay.
A slice or a dtype view of a received view crosses by value.

| Python sends | R sees | Back in Python | Notes |
|----|----|----|----|
| uint8 | raw | uint8 | exact |
| int8 / int16 / uint16 | integer | int32 | widened, values exact |
| int32 | integer | int32 | exact |
| uint32 | double | float64 | exact |
| int64 | integer64 | int64 | exact |
| uint64, ≤ ±2^53 | double | float64 | dtype lost, values exact |
| uint64, past ±2^53 | `NA` | NaN | lost on the first hop |
| float32 | double | float64 | widened, values exact |
| float64 | double | float64 | exact |
| bool | logical | `bool_` (int32 with NAs) | dtype lost |
| complex64 / complex128 | complex | complex128 | exact |
| timedelta64 | `difftime` | timedelta64[us] | unit normalizes to us, values exact |

| R sends | Python sees | Back in R | Notes |
|----|----|----|----|
| integer | int32 (float64 with NAs) | integer | exact |
| integer64 (bit64) | int64 (warns on `NA`) | integer64 | exact; a genuine Python `-2^63` arrives as `NA` |
| double | float64 | double | exact |
| raw | uint8 | raw | exact |
| complex | complex128 | complex | exact |
| logical | `bool_` (int32 with NAs) | **integer** | the logical tag is lost on a Python round trip (the values are not); a whole view sent back crosses by reference and stays logical |
| difftime | timedelta64[us] | difftime (secs) | units normalize to seconds, values exact; `NA` crosses as `NaT` |

Between two Python processes — a channel or a pool — the conversions on this
page never run: the identity dtypes cross unchanged and everything else
pickles, so an exact Python-to-Python send of a non-identity dtype needs no
work.
They apply only when the other end runs R.
